Volume 12 · Chapter 05

Panel data and longitudinal identification

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v12-c04

By the endEvaluate within-unit identification and dynamic-panel assumptions.

Volume 12 · Chapter 5

Panel data and longitudinal identification

Following the same unit over time offers a way to remove a persistent omitted characteristic. It does not turn the remaining variation into an experiment. A future explanatory variable may reveal today's disturbance; a missing follow-up may select high outcomes; and a shock shared by a thousand firms is still one shock. The transformation, the population question and the sampling argument must agree.

Capability. Derive within, known-covariance random-effects and balanced correlated-effects estimators; distinguish the assumptions that identify their targets from those that support inference; prove a fixed-time dynamic-panel failure and a valid lagged moment; recover a population mean under an explicit attrition model; and diagnose a common shock that defeats both unit and date effects. All cases are original finite teaching laws, not empirical findings.

Prerequisites. Chapter 1 supplies fixed-dimensional iid laws of large numbers, central limits, delta methods and continuous matrix inversion. Chapter 2 supplies projections, GLS and unit-score covariance arguments. Chapter 3 supplies fixed-dimensional moment estimation and rank. Chapter 4 distinguishes conditional models, likelihood and selection assumptions. We use fixed T and an increasing number N of whole units unless explicitly declaring a different counterexample; there is no automatic joint large-N, large-T theorem.

1. Remove an effect; then justify the remaining score

For unit i and date t=1,…,T, let yᵢₜ be a scalar outcome, xᵢₜ a p-dimensional column, cᵢ a time-constant unobserved effect, and uᵢₜ an idiosyncratic disturbance. The proposed structural equation is yᵢₜ=xᵢₜ′β+cᵢ+uᵢₜ. Stack dates as yᵢ=Xᵢβ+cᵢ1+uᵢ, with Xᵢ of dimension T×p and 1 the T-vector of ones. p and T are fixed, T≥2; the variables' units determine the units of β. A prime denotes transpose. Define P=11′/T and M=I−P. Both are symmetric projections, M1=0 and MP=0. A bar denotes a within-unit date average; thus (MXᵢ)ₜ=xᵢₜ′−x̄ᵢ′.

For any proposed slope b, the least-squares minimizing unit intercept is aᵢ(b)=ȳᵢ−x̄ᵢ′b. Substituting into ∑ᵢ‖yᵢ−Xᵢb−aᵢ1‖² gives ∑ᵢ‖M(yᵢ−Xᵢb)‖². Differentiation yields the within estimator, exactly equal to least squares with a separate dummy for each unit (LSDV), provided its within Gram matrix is invertible:

β̂FE=(∑ᵢXᵢ′MXᵢ)−1∑ᵢXᵢ′Myᵢ,
β̂FE−β=Q̂−1N−1∑ᵢgᵢ, where Hᵢ=Xᵢ′MXᵢ, Q̂=N−1∑ᵢHᵢ, gᵢ=Xᵢ′Muᵢ.

The minimizer is unique precisely when ∑Hᵢ is positive definite: a′∑Hᵢa=∑‖MXᵢa‖². A time-constant regressor has MXᵢa=0 and cannot be separated from unrestricted cᵢ by this estimator. Include neither a common intercept nor such a column in the invertible within slope matrix. Fitted unit levels can be recovered, but with fixed T each individual cᵢ estimate generally retains disturbance noise. Merely introducing more unit dummies does not estimate each effect consistently.

Three different mean restrictions. Contemporaneous exogeneity means E[uᵢₜ|xᵢₜ,cᵢ]=0. Sequential exogeneity here means E[uᵢₜ|xᵢ₁,…,xᵢₜ,cᵢ]=0: current disturbances may affect future regressors. Strict exogeneity means E[uᵢₜ|Xᵢ,cᵢ]=0 for every date. These are conditional means, not independence assertions. Strict exogeneity implies the other two, but not conversely. Since demeaning a regressor uses future dates, contemporaneous or sequential exogeneity alone need not center Xᵢ′Muᵢ. The exact weaker identification condition for this within moment is E[gᵢ]=0 together with within rank; strict exogeneity is a transparent sufficient condition.

Fixed-T theorem and proof. Assume the whole vectors (Xᵢ,cᵢ,uᵢ) are iid across units; cᵢ is finite almost surely; E‖Xᵢ‖⁴ and E‖uᵢ‖⁴ are finite; strict exogeneity holds; and Q=E[Hᵢ] is positive definite. Norms are Euclidean/Frobenius. Within each unit the disturbances may be serially dependent and heteroskedastic. Conditional expectation centers gᵢ. The norm bounds ‖Hᵢ‖≤‖Xᵢ‖² and ‖gᵢ‖≤‖Xᵢ‖‖uᵢ‖ show E‖Hᵢ‖² and E‖gᵢ‖² are finite by Cauchy–Schwarz. The iid law gives Q̂→Q and N⁻¹∑gᵢ→0. Positive definiteness makes Q̂ invertible with probability tending to one; define an arbitrary value on its finite-sample singular event for the limit argument, but report that event as failure in a computation. The exact identity above proves consistency. The iid vector CLT applied to one score per unit then gives

√N(β̂FE−β) ⇒ Normal(0,V),
B=E[gᵢgᵢ′], V=Q−1BQ−1.

The fourth-moment assumptions are sufficient rather than necessary; direct square-integrability of Hᵢ and gᵢ plus a centered score also suffices for this argument. They do not require any moment of cᵢ beyond what is needed to define the model, because M removes it exactly. The statement is about a common coefficient in the stipulated equation. A heterogeneous-effect within projection would require its own target analysis.

Feasible covariance, including its replacement proof. Set ĝᵢ=Xᵢ′M(yᵢ−Xᵢβ̂)=gᵢ−Hᵢδ, δ=β̂−β, and B̂=N⁻¹∑ĝᵢĝᵢ′. The difference between B̂ and N⁻¹∑gᵢgᵢ′ has norm at most 2‖δ‖N⁻¹∑‖gᵢ‖‖Hᵢ‖+‖δ‖²N⁻¹∑‖Hᵢ‖². Both averages are Op(1) by the stated moments; δ=op(1), so this difference tends to zero. An iid law handles the true-score average. Therefore V̂=Q̂⁻¹B̂Q̂⁻¹→V. The covariance estimate for β̂ is V̂/N. Studentize a fixed contrast only when its limiting variance is positive. This is an asymptotic unit-score argument, not exact Student t inference, a solution to few units, or permission to treat NT rows as independent. See the inspected MIT panel notes for the within/unit-score framework; the explicit moment and replacement conditions here delimit our result.

Worked example 1: a persistent effect changes pooled regression

Let b,d,e₁,e₂ be four independent fair signs, giving 16 equiprobable unit states. Set T=2, c=b, x=(b−d,b+d), and yₜ=c+2xₜ+eₜ. Repeat whole units independently. The true slope is 2. Since E∑xₜ²=4 and E∑xₜyₜ=10, the pooled through-origin projection is 5/2. All relevant means are zero, so adding a population common intercept gives the same slope. The excess 1/2 comes from E∑xₜc=2, not from the idiosyncratic disturbances.

Within transformation leaves x̃=(−d,d), so H=2 in every state. Its score is g=d(e₂−e₁), with Eg=0 and E[g²]=2. Thus Q=2, V=1/2 and the within target is 2. In fact β̂=2+(2N)⁻¹∑dᵢ(eᵢ₂−eᵢ₁); it is exactly unbiased with variance 1/(2N) under this finite law. This finite variance identity does not make the standardized statistic exactly normal. Adding a time-constant recorded covariate b does not let within regression identify its own slope separately from c.

2. Random-effects weights are not an exogeneity repair

A different model writes the composite disturbance vᵢ=aᵢ1+uᵢ after including any identified common mean in the regressors. If Var(vᵢ|Xᵢ)=Ω=σᵤ²I+σₐ²11′, with σᵤ²>0 and σₐ²≥0, then Ω=σᵤ²M+(σᵤ²+Tσₐ²)P. Orthogonality of M and P gives its inverse without a matrix-inversion guess:

Ω−1=M/σᵤ²+P/(σᵤ²+Tσₐ²),
A=M+(1−θ)P=I−θP, θ=1−√[σᵤ²/(σᵤ²+Tσₐ²)],
A′A=σᵤ²Ω−1.

Consequently GLS is ordinary least squares after quasi-demeaning yᵢₜ−θȳᵢ and xᵢₜ−θx̄ᵢ, including the transformed intercept 1−θ if present. Both the within and between directions receive positive weight for finite parameters. At σₐ²=0, θ=0 and the transformation is pooled OLS. As σₐ²/σᵤ²→∞, θ→1 and the weighting approaches within projection; the limiting covariance is not a finite invertible covariance, and the limiting weighting matrix loses the constant direction. Only identified within slopes have a within limit under the corresponding rank condition.

Consistency and efficiency require different restrictions. With fixed known working W positive definite, finite displayed moments and a positive-definite weighted Gram, the population slope solves E[Xᵢ′WXᵢ]βW=E[Xᵢ′Wyᵢ]. The identifying mean condition is E[Xᵢ′Wvᵢ]=0. A sufficient random-effects model is E[aᵢ|Xᵢ]=0 and E[uᵢ|Xᵢ,aᵢ]=0. Under iid whole units and integrable weighted Gram and score, their laws of large numbers prove consistency just as in section 1. Mean orthogonality alone does not imply the compound conditional covariance; that covariance plus exogeneity and uncorrelated units is what justifies the known-Ω GLS efficiency comparison among linear unbiased estimators. Conversely, a plausible variance formula does not center a score contaminated by correlated heterogeneity. We derive only known-parameter weighting here, not a universal feasible variance-component theorem.

Worked example 2: a working covariance leaves an omitted-effect bias

Return to the 16-state law of example 1. Use the deliberately working matrix Ω=I+11′ at T=2, so W=Ω⁻¹=I−11′/3 and θ=1−1/√3. This is not the true conditional covariance model: c=b is known from the regressor history through x̄=b. The weighted Gram expectation is 8/3. The omitted-effect moment is E[X′Wc1]=2/3, and the weighted outcome moment is 2(8/3)+2/3=6. The working random-effects target is therefore 9/4, between the within value 2 and pooled value 5/2, but still different from the stipulated structural coefficient.

In this law E[c|X]=x̄=b. The correctly specified population regression on xₜ and x̄ has coefficients 2 and 1, respectively, and intercept zero. Its interpretation uses that explicit conditional mean. A smaller standard error around 9/4 would not answer the original slope question.

3. What correlated-effects equivalence actually proves

Consider a balanced sample and a scalar weight wᵢ>0 shared by all T observations of unit i. Regress yᵢₜ on a common intercept, xᵢₜ and x̄ᵢ. Exclude a constant column from x itself, and assume both the weighted within Gram matrix and the between Gram for (1,x̄ᵢ′) have full rank. Write the fitted value as α+x̃ᵢₜ′b+x̄ᵢ′(b+d), where d is the coefficient on the added mean. The weighted squared-error objective decomposes exactly:

∑ᵢwᵢ∑ₜ(yᵢₜ−α−xᵢₜ′b−x̄ᵢ′d)²
=∑ᵢwᵢ‖Myᵢ−MXᵢb‖²+T∑ᵢwᵢ[ȳᵢ−α−x̄ᵢ′(b+d)]².

The cross term vanishes because each within vector sums to zero. The one-to-one reparameterization (b,d)↔(b,b+d) separates the two minimizations. Therefore the coefficient b on the dated regressor is exactly the common-weight within coefficient. The mean coefficient d is the between coefficient minus that within coefficient. Rank of the two separate blocks also proves full rank of the combined transformed design. This is finite-sample algebra, with no exogeneity needed for the equality.

For structural interpretation, impose E[cᵢ|Xᵢ]=α+x̄ᵢ′π together with strict idiosyncratic exogeneity, finite second moments of the augmented regressors and outcomes, and a positive-definite population augmented Gram. Then E[yᵢ|Xᵢ]=Xᵢβ+1(α+x̄ᵢ′π), and the conditional-mean regression identifies β and π. A linear projection of c on x̄ only makes its residual orthogonal to x̄; it need not make that residual orthogonal to every dated x. Do not turn a projection statement into this conditional-mean model. If heterogeneity depends on different date-specific combinations, more structure is needed. Time-constant covariate effects also need restrictions beyond unrestricted within identification.

The sample identity stated here uses a common balanced observation set and common within-unit weights. Different outcome-specific samples, varying date weights, nonlinear links or arbitrary missing histories do not inherit this proof. A test contrasting estimators cannot establish exogeneity merely by failing to reject; its covariance, identified coordinates and null distribution need their own argument. We do not invoke a generic robust Hausman chi-square result. These distinctions follow the inspected Imbens–Wooldridge lecture scope, with the finite-sample equality proved above.

Worked example 3: the equality in a noisy weighted sample

Three units have b=(−1,0,2), d=(1,2,1), weights w=(1,2,1), xᵢ=(bᵢ−dᵢ,bᵢ+dᵢ), and yᵢₜ=1+3bᵢ+2xᵢₜ+eᵢₜ. The realized disturbances are (1,−1), (0,2), (−2,0). These are specified sample numbers, not a new stochastic exogeneity assumption.

UnitWeightx₁,x₂y₁,y₂x̄ȳ
11−2,0−5,−3−1−4
22−2,2−3,702
311,37,13210

The within denominator is ∑wᵢ(Δxᵢ)²/2=20 and numerator ∑wᵢΔxᵢΔyᵢ/2=48, so the slope is 12/5. Weighted between means are x̄w=1/4 and ȳw=5/2; the centered between cross product is 43/2 and centered Gram is 19/4. Its slope is 86/19 and intercept 26/19. The regression on (1,x,x̄) therefore has coefficients (26/19,12/5,202/95), since 86/19−12/5=202/95. Neither realized slope must equal its population structural value. The within/CRE equality nevertheless holds exactly for this common sample and these weights.

4. A lagged outcome changes the orthogonality question

Suppose yᵢₜ=ρyᵢ,ₜ₋₁+cᵢ+uᵢₜ. Even if the innovation has conditional mean zero given the entire past, a future regressor contains today's innovation. This violates the strict history restriction used to justify within transformation. A transformation that removes cᵢ can therefore introduce correlation between its transformed regressor and disturbance. The inspected Arellano notes distinguish these information sets and unit-level dynamic moments; our exact finite construction supplies its own initial conditions and calculations.

Worked example 4: exact fixed-T bias and a different valid moment

Set cᵢ=0, yᵢ₀=0, yᵢ₁=eᵢ₁ and yᵢ₂=ρeᵢ₁+eᵢ₂, with independent fair innovations and independent units. Fit unit effects using the two transitions t=1,2, so the regressor vector is (0,eᵢ₁). At each unit its within Gram is 1/2; its within slope contribution is ρ−1+eᵢ₁eᵢ₂. Consequently

ρ̂FE=ρ−1+N−1∑ᵢeᵢ₁eᵢ₂,
Eρ̂FE=ρ−1, Var(ρ̂FE)=1/N, plim ρ̂FE=ρ−1.

At ρ=1/2 the estimator concentrates around −1/2. Its error relative to ρ is not removed by increasing N. There was no omitted unit effect in this example; unnecessarily estimating fixed effects still uses the endogenous transformed regressor. This is an original two-transition counterexample, not a stationary dynamic-panel bias formula.

Now observe one more transition yᵢ₃=ρyᵢ₂+eᵢ₃ with an independent fair eᵢ₃. Difference the third equation: Δyᵢ₃=ρΔyᵢ₂+(eᵢ₃−eᵢ₂). The instrument zᵢ=yᵢ₁=eᵢ₁ is orthogonal to both innovations in the difference. The three signs give eight equiprobable states. Direct expectation gives

E[zᵢ(eᵢ₃−eᵢ₂)]=0, B=E[zᵢΔyᵢ₂]=ρ−1,
E[zᵢΔyᵢ₃]=ρ(ρ−1), E[{zᵢ(eᵢ₃−eᵢ₂)}²]=2.

When ρ≠1 the moment identifies ρ. The ratio estimator ∑zΔy₃/∑zΔy₂ is consistent, and its exact ratio expansion gives √N(ρ̂IV−ρ)⇒Normal(0,2/(ρ−1)²). At ρ=1/2, B=−1/2, the numerator moment is −1/4 and the limiting variance is 8. A feasible variance uses the sample squared unit moments and denominator, as in Chapter 3. A sample denominator can equal zero even when the population rank is positive; the computation must report it rather than divide blindly.

At ρ=1, this instrument's population moment is zero for every proposed slope, so this moment does not identify the parameter. That is not a claim that no other feature of the data can identify it. As ρ approaches 1 along changing populations, the fixed-parameter normal approximation need not remain uniform. No weak-instrument limit or system-GMM moment is derived here.

The valid lag restriction, stated precisely. For a general fixed-T model assume integrable products and E[uᵢₜ|cᵢ,yᵢ₀,…,yᵢ,ₜ₋₁]=0. If zᵢ is measurable with respect to (cᵢ,yᵢ₀,…,yᵢ,ₜ₋₂) and has appropriate second moments, iterated expectation gives E[zᵢuᵢₜ]=E[zᵢuᵢ,ₜ₋₁]=0. Hence it centers the differenced error. A dated outcome yᵢ,ₜ₋₁ generally does not. Instrument validity, nonzero rank and finite score variance are separate conditions. Stacking finitely many such moments uses one vector per independent unit. Even independent innovations yield Cov(uₜ−uₜ₋₁,uₜ₊₁−uₜ)=−Var(uₜ) when their variances are equal; differenced rows are not independent. Serial innovation dependence or a different initial law must be checked directly before reusing any moment.

5. Attrition changes the population unless the observation process is modeled

Let H be a baseline cell observed for everyone in an iid cohort. It takes finitely many values h with probabilities πₕ>0. Let W contain the full outcome information, Y a component of W, and R indicate that the follow-up outcome is observed. The observed record is (H,R,RY), with the response flag distinguishing a missing value from a zero outcome. For a moment to be identified from this record, require that ψ(W) can be calculated from (H,Y) whenever R=1; for the mean below, ψ(W)=Y. Assume E|ψ(W)|<∞ and the specific missing-at-random restriction

E[R|W,H]=p(H), with p(h)≥ε>0 for all cells.
E[Rψ(W)/p(H)]=E{E[R|W,H]ψ(W)/p(H)}=E[ψ(W)].

The equality follows by conditional expectation; bounded inverse probabilities ensure integrability. This identifies the full-cohort moment, not merely the respondent moment. Baseline information must be available for nonrespondents too. Positivity alone does not give finite variance; for the mean calculations below assume E[Y²]<∞. Nor does positivity imply the conditional response restriction: selection on the unobserved outcome can invalidate the identity despite strictly positive cell response rates. The inspected Wooldridge working paper treats a broader selection framework. We prove only this finite-cell MAR case and do not import its general nuisance-estimation theorem.

Estimating cell response probabilities changes the influence. Write μₕ=E[Y|H=h], μ=∑πₕμₕ. Let Nₕ count baseline units in cell h and Nₕᴿ its respondents. When each cell has respondents, p̂ₕ=Nₕᴿ/Nₕ and

μ̂cell=N−1∑ᵢRᵢYᵢ/p̂Hᵢ=∑ₕ(Nₕ/N)Ȳₕᴿ.

This estimator uses the sample's baseline cell frequencies, not fixed known πₕ. To derive its expansion, set π̂ₕ=Nₕ/N, âₕ=N⁻¹∑1{Hᵢ=h}RᵢYᵢ and b̂ₕ=N⁻¹∑1{Hᵢ=h}Rᵢ. The estimator is the smooth function ∑π̂ₕâₕ/b̂ₕ at the population point (πₕ,πₕpₕμₕ,πₕpₕ), whose denominators are positive. Its derivatives are μₕ, 1/pₕ and −μₕ/pₕ. Finite second moments give a fixed-dimensional iid CLT for all these averages; the delta expansion has remainder op(N⁻¹ᐟ²). Combining the centered terms yields

√N(μ̂cell−μ)=N−1/2∑ᵢφᵢ+op(1),
φᵢ=μHᵢ−μ+[Rᵢ/p(Hᵢ)](Yᵢ−μHᵢ),
Vcell=Var(μH)+E[Var(Y|H)/p(H)].

The residual component has conditional mean zero given H; MAR gives its conditional second moment Var(Y|H)/p(H), proving the last formula and zero cross term. The first term of φ represents uncertainty in the population composition. If π were known and fixed in a differently defined estimator, that term would be absent. Let ŝₕ² be the respondent average of (Y−Ȳₕᴿ)², using denominator Nₕᴿ. A feasible estimate is V̂cell=∑π̂ₕ(Ȳₕᴿ−μ̂cell)²+∑π̂ₕŝₕ²/p̂ₕ. Finite-cell laws of large numbers for respondent counts, Y and Y² prove its consistency under the same finite second moments; report standard error √(V̂cell/N).

A positive-probability cell may have zero respondents in a finite sample. The displayed ratio is then unavailable; report the missing cell and do not invent a mean. For an everywhere-defined asymptotic sequence, assign any fixed finite value on the event that any Nₕᴿ=0. That event has probability at most ∑ₕ(1−πₕpₕ)ᴺ→0, so it does not change the expansion in probability. This convention is a proof device, not an imputation recommendation. An absent baseline cell also has no respondents and is included in this declared failure event.

With genuinely known p, the unnormalized Horvitz–Thompson estimator N⁻¹∑RY/p has influence RY/p−μ and variance VHT=E[Y²/p(H)]−μ². Its difference from φ is μH(R/p−1), orthogonal to φ under the stipulated MAR law. Therefore VHT−Vcell=E[μH²(1−p)/p]≥0 in this particular saturated finite-cell comparison. This is not a general theorem that estimated propensities always improve efficiency. It compares these two precise estimators of the same target. A normalized known-p ratio estimator is a third estimator with a different influence.

Worked example 5: whom did the follow-up lose?

H is a fair 0/1 baseline cell; V is an independent fair sign. Let Y=2+4H+V. All H=0 units respond; H=1 units independently respond with probability 1/3, conditional on H and independently of V. There are six latent atoms: (H=0,R=1,V=±1) with probability 1/4 each; (H=1,R=1,V=±1) with probability 1/12 each; and (H=1,R=0,V=±1) with probability 1/6 each. The last two atoms merge in the observed record, leaving five observable atoms. Missing Y is not a recorded zero.

The cohort mean is 4 and variance is 5. Response probability is 2/3 and E[RY]=2, so the respondent mean is 3. Cell response weighting restores the target 4. Its influence variance is Var(2+4H)+E[1/p(H)]=4+(1+3)/2=6. The known-p unnormalized estimator has variance (5+3·37)/2−16=42. The difference 36 equals (1/2)·6²·(1−1/3)/(1/3). The coefficient 6 is a root-N variance, so the large-sample variance of the fitted-cell estimate is 6/N, not 6 per observed row.

To expose the identification assumption, hold the entire observable law fixed but set every missing outcome to 3 in law A and to 9 in law B. The common observed contribution E[RY] is 2 and missing mass is 1/3, so the full means become 3 and 5, respectively. Both have exactly the same baseline counts, response flags and observed outcomes. Neither modified law satisfies the preceding MAR restriction. No analysis of the observed records alone can distinguish these two unrestricted missing-outcome means.

6. Unit effects and date effects do not create independent units

Suppose uᵢₜ=λᵢFₜ+εᵢₜ. Subtracting each date's cross-sectional mean removes a common loading only when all λᵢ are equal: the remaining factor term is (λᵢ−λ̄)Fₜ. In a balanced equal-weight panel, subtracting both unit and date means and adding back the grand mean leaves (λᵢ−λ̄)(Fₜ−F̄), plus the similarly transformed ε. This follows by expanding the four averages. Time effects absorb a homogeneous additive common shock, not arbitrary heterogeneous exposure to that shock.

Worked example 6: twice demeaning still leaves one random shock

Use a fixed balanced design q=(−1,−1,1,1), s=(−1,1), and xᵢₜ=qᵢsₜ. Let a single fair sign U determine uᵢₜ=qᵢsₜU for every unit, and yᵢₜ=2xᵢₜ+uᵢₜ. The regressor and error already have zero unit means, zero date means and zero grand mean. Both within and two-way demeaning leave them unchanged. The estimated slope is exactly 2+U: it is 1 or 3 with equal probabilities.

Repeat the balanced q pattern as N grows while keeping the same common U. Every unit has Hᵢ=2 and gᵢ=2U, so Q̂=2 and N⁻¹∑gᵢ=2U. The score mean is zero over repeated draws of U, yet its average does not converge to zero: Var(N⁻¹∑gᵢ)=4 because every pair has score covariance 4. The slope error has variance 1 for every N. The independent-unit hypothesis of section 1 is false. Fitted residuals happen to be zero, so a mechanically applied residual unit-score covariance is zero; that does not erase the random coefficient error.

If the shock instead entered as uᵢₜ=sₜU with homogeneous loading, date means would remove it completely in this fixed design. That is a different law. Conditioning on U in the original law changes the conditional projection slope to 2+U; it does not identify the original 2 by relabeling the same regression. Additional factor structure, independent shocks, or a different time-asymptotic argument would need their own identification and inference proof.

Cross-unit dependence is not repaired by choosing a different covariance menu after estimation. Neither a generic two-way-cluster formula nor interactive-factor consistency is proved here. First identify the source of repeated independent information and the precise target conditional or unconditional on common shocks. The aggregate-shock warning in the inspected Arellano source supports this distinction; the finite counterexample makes it explicit without an empirical frequency claim.

7. Derive, transfer and critique

Show assumptions and intermediate identities, not only a named estimator. Treat all finite laws below as original teaching specifications. A correct arithmetic result attached to an invalid identification argument is not a correct solution.

  1. Derive the within/LSDV equality from the least-squares objective. Give the necessary sample rank condition. Explain why a recorded time-constant regressor and each individual unit effect are not consistently learned merely by increasing N with fixed T.
  2. For the 16-state law in example 1, compute the pooled through-origin target, within target, unit Gram, score variance and exact finite-N within variance. Would appending b as another within regressor identify its separate coefficient?
  3. Let z,e₁,e₂ be independent fair signs, c=0, x₁=z, x₂=e₁ and yₜ=βxₜ+eₜ. Repeat units independently. Verify sequential and contemporaneous exogeneity but refute strict exogeneity. Compute the probability limit of the two-date within slope.
  4. For T=3, σᵤ²=4 and σₐ²=1, derive θ and Ω⁻¹. State their action on the constant vector and on x=(−1,0,1)′. Explain which mean and covariance restrictions turn the weights into a consistent, efficient GLS procedure and what changes at σₐ²=0.
  5. Reconstruct every coefficient in example 3 using the within and between decompositions. Prove why the dated-regressor coefficient equals the weighted within coefficient. State the additional condition needed to interpret the added mean coefficient as a conditional heterogeneity coefficient.
  6. In example 4 at ρ=1/2, derive the exact two-transition FE distribution's mean and variance. For the additional third transition derive the lag-IV numerator, denominator, moment variance and root-N limit variance. Explain why differenced rows cannot be treated as independent observations.
  7. Keep example 4's initial law. Compute lag-IV root-N variance at ρ=0 and at ρ=9/10, and explain the rank boundary at ρ=1. Separately set e₃=e₁ while retaining independent fair e₁,e₂ and ρ=1/2. Recompute the instrument's error moment and ratio target; identify the violated assumption.
  8. Prove the finite-cell MAR weighted-moment identity and derive the fitted-cell mean influence, including estimated baseline frequencies. For example 5 compute the fitted-cell and known-p unnormalized root-N variances and explain their difference. Do not use the oracle variance for the fitted estimator.
  9. In example 5 change only the H=1 response probability from 1/3 to 1/2. Compute the respondent target, fitted-cell variance and known-p unnormalized variance. For N=2 compute the probability that at least one baseline cell has no respondents. Then explain why the original example's observed law cannot distinguish full means 3 and 5 without MAR.
  10. Prove both demeaning results in example 6. Compute the variance of the average unit score and the residual-based unit-score covariance. Compare homogeneous loadings. Why does conditioning on the common U not recover the same target?
  11. Under section 1's assumptions, prove B̂→B using ĝᵢ=gᵢ−Hᵢδ. State the normalization for the covariance of β̂ and the additional condition for a fixed contrast's studentization. Identify exactly which step fails in example 6; changing a finite-sample multiplier is not an answer.
  12. A study follows eight firms for three dates, regresses outcomes on lagged outcomes and chosen investment, adds firm and date effects, discards nonresponding firms, and reports row-iid standard errors. It concludes that investment causes growth because a random-effects comparison test did not reject. Give six distinct objections tied to identification or inference, two feasible redesigns or sensitivity analyses with limited claims, and a concise conclusion the existing design could honestly support. The rubric below allocates 12 points.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. For fixed b, differentiating in aᵢ gives T aᵢ=∑ₜ(yᵢₜ−xᵢₜ′b), hence aᵢ=ȳᵢ−x̄ᵢ′b. Substitution gives ∑‖M(yᵢ−Xᵢb)‖². Its normal equation is (∑Xᵢ′MXᵢ)b=∑Xᵢ′Myᵢ. Uniqueness requires ∑‖MXᵢa‖²>0 for every nonzero a. A time-constant column is annihilated, so its slope is confounded with arbitrary unit levels. Even with β known, the fitted effect is cᵢ+ūᵢ; fixed T leaves the same noise in that particular unit as other units are added. These are distinct rank and consistency limitations.

  2. Each xₜ has second moment 2, giving pooled denominator 4. E∑xₜc=E[2b²]=2, and E∑xₜeₜ=0, so the numerator is 2·4+2=10 and target 5/2. Within x̃=(−d,d) gives H=2 and g=d(e₂−e₁). Since Ed²=1, E(e₂−e₁)²=2, Eg=0 and E[g²]=2. Within target 2 and root-N variance (1/2)·2·(1/2)=1/2 follow. The exact estimator averages independent scores with constant denominator 2, so its variance is 1/(2N). Appended b vanishes under M, making the enlarged within Gram singular.

  3. E[e₁|z]=0 and E[e₂|z,e₁]=0 establish the sequential restriction; their coarser contemporaneous versions also hold. But E[e₁|x₁,x₂]=x₂=e₁, not zero, so strict exogeneity fails. Δx=e₁−z and Δe=e₂−e₁ have E(Δx)²=2 and E[ΔxΔe]=−1. Within least squares equals the difference slope with both cross products divided by 2, so its probability limit is β−1/2. Whole-unit independence gives these laws of large numbers; no causal conclusion follows from observing the chronological order alone.

  4. The between eigenvalue is 4+3=7 and the within eigenvalue is 4. Hence θ=1−2/√7 and Ω⁻¹=M/4+P/7=I/4−11′/28. It maps 1 to 1/7 and x=(−1,0,1)′ to x/4. Quasi-demeaning maps 1 to 2·1/√7 and leaves x unchanged; A′A=4Ω⁻¹. E[v|X]=0 is a sufficient mean restriction for consistency when the weighted Gram has rank, while the actual conditional covariance Ω underpins GLS efficiency. The compound formula used merely as a working weight does not remove correlated effects. At σₐ²=0, θ=0 and Ω⁻¹=I/4: OLS weighting with a scalar factor.

  5. The table implies within denominator 20 and numerator 48, so b=12/5. Weighted averages of the unit means are 1/4 and 5/2. The between centered Gram is 19/4 and cross product 43/2, hence slope k=86/19, intercept 5/2−(86/19)(1/4)=26/19, and added mean coefficient d=k−b=202/95. Reparameterizing by (b,k=b+d) makes within and between residuals orthogonal under the same wᵢ at every date. Full rank gives the unique stated coefficients. To read d as π, require E[c|X]=α+x̄′π and E[u|X,c]=0, not just a projection of c onto x̄ or this realized algebraic equality.

  6. The two-transition differences are Δx=e₁ and Δy=(ρ−1)e₁+e₂. Since e₁²=1, FE equals ρ−1+N⁻¹∑e₁e₂. At ρ=1/2 its mean is −1/2 and variance 1/N. For the third transition, z=e₁, Δy₂=(ρ−1)e₁+e₂ and Δy₃=ρΔy₂+e₃−e₂. Thus B=ρ−1=−1/2, E[zΔy₃]=ρB=−1/4 and E[z(e₃−e₂)]=0. Squaring the latter unit score gives expectation 2, so the root-N IV variance is 2/B²=8. Adjacent differenced errors share e₂ with opposite signs and covariance −1. A stacked moment vector can retain that covariance; treating its rows as independent discards it.

  7. At ρ=0, B=−1 and variance 2; at ρ=9/10, B=−1/10 and variance 200. These are fixed-parameter limits, not a guarantee of good finite-sample coverage near rank failure. At ρ=1, B=0 and the population lag moment vanishes for all candidate slopes. In the separate serial-dependence perturbation e₃=e₁, E[e₁(e₃−e₂)]=1. At ρ=1/2 the denominator remains −1/2, while the numerator becomes ρB+1=3/4. The ratio target is −3/2. The innovation is no longer mean zero given the past, so the old moment is invalid; the instrument's date alone did not guarantee exclusion.

  8. By MAR, E[Rψ/p|W,H]=ψ, and integrability justifies expectation. Identification from (H,R,RY) also uses the stated requirement that ψ is computable from (H,Y) for respondents; the algebraic identity alone does not make an unobserved moment observable. The finite-cell estimate is ∑π̂ₕâₕ/b̂ₕ. Differentiation at (πₕ,πₕpₕμₕ,πₕpₕ) gives derivatives (μₕ,1/pₕ,−μₕ/pₕ). Combining their empirical fluctuations yields φ=μ_H−μ+R(Y−μ_H)/p_H. The finite positive denominators and second moments justify the delta remainder. Under MAR the two parts are orthogonal, yielding variance 4+2=6 in example 5. Known-p unnormalized weighting instead has influence RY/p−4, variance E[Y²/p]−16=(5+111)/2−16=42. The difference 36 is the variance of μ_H(R/p−1), which is orthogonal to φ. The first term of φ must not be dropped: baseline composition is estimated from the cohort.

  9. Response probability becomes 3/4 and E[RY]=1+(1/2)(1/2)6=5/2, so the respondent target is 10/3. The full mean stays 4. Fitted-cell variance is 4+(1+2)/2=11/2. Known-p unnormalized variance is (5+2·37)/2−16=47/2. The two response-cell probabilities are 1/2 and 1/4; missing response mass is 1/4. Inclusion–exclusion gives P(any response cell empty)=(1/2)²+(3/4)²−(1/4)²=3/4 for N=2. Population positivity therefore does not guarantee computability in a tiny sample. In the original law, missing mass 1/3 is invisible apart from its flag. Filling it with 3 or 9 yields 2+(1/3)3=3 or 2+(1/3)9=5, with identical observed distributions. Only additional assumptions such as the stated MAR restriction rule out those alternatives.

  10. Since ∑qᵢ=0 and ∑sₜ=0, x=qᵢsₜ and u=qᵢsₜU have zero row and column averages. Within and two-way transformations leave both unchanged, giving β̂=2+U. Each gᵢ=2U, so the average score has variance 4, including all off-diagonal covariances. At the fitted slope y−Xβ̂ is identically zero, hence the residual unit-score covariance is zero despite Var(β̂−2)=1. With homogeneous loading u=sₜU, date demeaning removes the shock. In the heterogeneous case, conditioning on U leaves E[y|X,U]=(2+U)x, so the conditional projection target itself differs from 2. Conditioning does not supply the missing independent variation.

  11. Expand (gᵢ−Hᵢδ)(gᵢ−Hᵢδ)′−gᵢgᵢ′ and apply the triangle inequality to get the section 1 bound. E‖H‖²<∞ and E‖g‖²<∞ imply E‖g‖‖H‖<∞. Iid laws make both bounding averages O_p(1), consistency gives δ=o_p(1), and the true-score average tends to B by its finite first moment. Thus B̂→B and V̂=Q̂⁻¹B̂Q̂⁻¹→V. Divide by N for the covariance of β̂. A fixed contrast a needs a′Va>0 for asymptotic normal studentization. In example 6 the independent-unit LLN for the score fails, δ=U does not tend to zero, and the joint error covariance has persistent cross-unit terms. A multiplier cannot repair those failures.

  12. Six distinctions, one point each. (1) Chosen investment can respond to current or anticipated shocks; fixed effects remove a constant level, not all time-varying confounding. (2) Lagged outcomes violate the full-history strict exogeneity required for the stated FE consistency proof; valid lag moments need explicit innovation/initial conditions and rank. (3) Complete-case selection changes the target unless a justified observation restriction and baseline information restore it; MAR and positivity are substantive assumptions. (4) Within-firm rows share shocks, so row-iid errors have no stated basis. (5) Common shocks with heterogeneous loadings can survive date effects; with only eight firms, even an independent-unit asymptotic approximation needs substantial caution. (6) Nonrejection of an estimator-comparison test does not prove either model's mean restriction, the test's calibration or causal interpretation.

    Two changes, two points each. For example, recover baseline histories and response flags for all firms, report response-cell support, and compare an explicitly justified MAR-weighted cohort target with transparent missing-outcome sensitivity. This can expose selection sensitivity but cannot verify MAR from observed outcomes. Separately, predefine investment timing/instruments from an economic assignment mechanism, test available first-stage rank descriptively, and use whole-firm moments with a stated innovation law; this addresses a specified moment, not every dynamic confounder or cross-firm shock. Other defensible choices include obtaining genuinely independent groups or more independent time variation under a newly justified time-series theorem. Award each change only if its required information and remaining limitation are stated.

    Conclusion, two points. The existing regression describes an association among the observed firms under its specified transformation. It does not yet establish an investment effect or calibrated uncertainty. A useful report distinguishes the cohort target, the actual observation process and the independent information source, and states which additional evidence would support each claim. No particular sign of the coefficient is required for credit.

8. Teach-back and delayed retrieval

Teach-back. In two minutes, explain why removing a unit effect, obtaining a centered moment and having many independent observations are three different achievements. Use one case from this chapter for each distinction.

Answer criteria

Demeaning algebraically removes cᵢ, but the dynamic or sequential-regressor example leaves a nonzero transformed score. A valid lagged instrument can center a moment, but its rank can vanish at ρ=1 under the declared initial law. Even a mean-zero unit score need not average out when every unit shares U. A satisfactory explanation identifies the target, the conditioning set and the source of independent repetition, rather than saying only that fixed effects control for everything or clustering fixes the model.

Delayed retention. Without the preceding solutions: (a) What does θ become when σₐ²=0? (b) In the dynamic law at ρ=0, what are the within probability limit and the valid lag-IV root-N variance? (c) In the attrition law with H=1 response probability 1/2, why are 11/2 and 47/2 different? (d) Does zero mean of the average common-shock score imply convergence to zero?

Retention answers

(a) θ=0, so quasi-demeaning reduces to pooled weighting. (b) The within limit is −1 and the valid lag-IV root-N variance is 2. (c) 11/2 belongs to the estimator that fits response probabilities by finite baseline cells and includes cell-frequency uncertainty; 47/2 belongs to known-p unnormalized weighting. They have different influence functions for the same full mean 4. (d) No. The common-shock score average is 2U, which has mean zero but variance 4 for every N and never approaches zero in probability.

9. Reproduce the finite evidence; respect the proof boundary

The companion source checker runs with python3 scripts/check_v12_c05.py in the source tree. It is silent on success; its importable check() returns a strict-JSON-compatible summary. It reconstructs the finite laws, weighted sample coefficients, dynamic moments, response influence variances, common-shock dependence and specified boundary failures. The four-file source package works from an unrelated current directory with ordinary or optimized Python and uses only the standard library. The checker is evidence for these finite computations, not a numerical proof of every asymptotic statement.

The source record reuses four explicitly scoped primary inspections: MIT 2017 panel notes, the 2014 Imbens–Wooldridge panel lecture, Arellano's revised 2009 predetermined-variable notes, and Wooldridge's 2004 missing-data working paper. Selected equation pages were inspected during source preparation; this chapter does not claim that every page of those documents was read. Our proofs are original within their stated sufficient conditions. We do not derive general stationary dynamic bias, system GMM, many-instrument asymptotics, arbitrary unbalanced/nonlinear CRE identities, a universal robust Hausman test, nonignorable-selection identification, interactive-factor inference or two-way-cluster validity. Such extensions require new hypotheses and separate arguments.

The next step is experimental design and randomized evaluation: choosing a source of identifying variation is a design decision, not an automatic consequence of having repeated measurements.

Sources and further study

  • 14.382 Spring 2017 Lecture 8: Linear Panel Data Models Under Strict and Weak Exogeneity — Within transformation and whole-unit covariance; distinction of strict versus sequential histories; finite-sample correlated-effects comparison. The chapter supplies its own sufficient moment conditions and proof.
  • Econometrics of Cross Section and Panel Data: Lecture 3, Linear Panel Data Models I — Conditional random-effects mean restrictions, full-history versus unit-mean heterogeneity, and limitations of estimator-comparison tests. The balanced common-weight identity is proved directly.
  • Dynamic Panel Data Models II: Lags and Predetermined Variables — Dynamic transformed-score endogeneity, past-information instruments and independent-unit GMM covariance; aggregate-shock limitations. The chapter proves only its explicit bounded finite-T laws.
  • Inverse probability weighted estimation for general missing data problems — Population selection weighting and the need to account for estimated response probabilities. The chapter independently derives a narrower finite-cell MAR influence and does not import the paper’s general theorem.
